issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of witnessed other trauma or with the rest of the profile. 'People cycling' and 'my ex' imply very different personal meanings, and neither has an evident connection to the reported threat items (general unsafety, sleep vigilance, hypervigilance). With only a weak Triggers → Threat link active, the triggers should still plausibly cue the threat state; these two triggers appear idiosyncratic in unrelated directions and are hard to reconcile as part of the same trauma-linked pattern.

vignette:
The event happened on a Tuesday night in late October. Sami was working the last run of the evening, a southbound commuter line that was usually quiet. He had just announced the final stop when he saw a man standing too close to the edge of the platform, arms wrapped around a woman who was struggling. Before Sami could do anything, the man pulled a knife and slashed her across the arm. Blood sprayed in an arc, catching the station lights. The woman staggered and fell, and Sami saw the deep, open wound on her forearm, the muscle and tendon exposed. He froze at the window of his cab, unable to look away, as the man fled and the woman screamed. That image—the blood, the torn skin, the wet sound of it hitting the concrete—had not faded in the two years since.

In the weeks that followed, Sami found himself scanning every platform as he pulled into a station, his eyes moving from face to face, looking for someone who might be holding a weapon or standing too close to the edge. He had always been a calm conductor, known for his steady voice over the intercom, but now he felt a constant hum of alertness that never turned off. Even when his supervisor assured him the station had new security cameras and more patrols, Sami could not believe it. He would nod, but inside he was certain that no amount of cameras could stop what he had seen. The feeling was worse at night. He would lie in bed, exhausted, but the moment he closed his eyes his body would tense, his ears straining for any sound. He had come to believe that if he let himself fall asleep, he would miss the warning signs—the scrape of a shoe, the click of a blade—and something terrible would happen again.

The most difficult moments came when something touched his skin unexpectedly. A cold draft from an open window in the cab, or the heat of a radiator brushing his arm, would make him flinch and look around wildly, his heart pounding. He knew it was irrational, but his body reacted before his mind could catch up. The temperature itself became a trigger, because it reminded him of the cold night air on his face when he first saw the blood, and the sudden heat that rushed through him when he realized what was happening. He began to avoid certain stations, ones where he had seen minor injuries before—a child with a scraped knee, a commuter with a bandaged hand—because the sight of visible wounds on others made his stomach drop and his vision narrow. He would radio for a substitute conductor to take over for a stop or two, claiming he needed a break, but the real reason was that he could not bear to look.

The hypervigilance bled into every part of his life. He stopped going to the grocery store after work because he could not stand the sight of the meat counter, the red of raw beef triggering the same visceral response. He ate microwave meals in his apartment, always sitting with his back to the wall. His sleep had become a series of short, restless naps punctuated by sudden awakenings. He had lost weight, and his supervisor had commented that he looked tired. Sami had brushed it off, but he knew he was running on fumes. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment on the job three weeks ago: he saw a teenager on the platform with a bloody nose, and he froze completely, unable to move or speak for nearly a minute. The train was delayed, and he had to be guided to the break room by a colleague. He was terrified that next time, he would not be able to function at all. He wanted to stop feeling like he was always one second away from disaster.
